definition.fact: Ordinary material samples, including gases, have mass and occupy space.

light-contrast.publisher: National Geographic Society, own education article updated19October2023
light-contrast.readScope: Actual main article and credits read; only the matter criteria and light contrast are used, not unviewed media or advanced cosmology.
light-contrast.fact: In the elementary matter classification, light is distinguished from material substances even though it carries energy.
light-contrast.limits: Do not equate not-matter with unreal or unable to affect things. No photon terminology, energy calculation, antimatter or BigBang narrative required.

solid.label: A small solid plastic block
givenFacts: The block is a material sample with mass.
It occupies space; two blocks cannot occupy the same ordinary position at the same time.
solid.expected: Matter: both criteria, not simply because it is visible or hard.

liquid.label: A cupful of liquid water, distinguished from its cup
givenFacts: The water has mass and takes up space.
Its shape changes with a suitable container.
liquid.expected: Matter: changing shape does not remove either criterion. The cup is also material, but is not the liquid being classified.

gas.label: Air trapped in an apparently empty capped bottle
givenFacts: Air is material with mass and occupies the available bottle space even when unseen.
Squeezing/air-bubble demonstrations can show that air occupies space; feel/resistance alone is not a measurement of mass.
gas.expected: Matter: invisibility is not absence. A balance below the required resolution cannot establish that a gas has no mass.

light.label: The light from a switched-on torch, distinguished from the torch
givenFacts: The torch and the illuminated wall are material objects.
Light is energy transferred from the torch and is not a material sample in this elementary classification.
light.expected: The objects are matter; emitted light is not a solid/liquid/gas substance. A lit patch on a wall is not proof that a new material now fills that patch.

property.label: The water’s temperature, distinguished from the water
givenFacts: Temperature describes a property of the water.
The temperature reading is not an additional material sample beside the water and thermometer.
property.expected: Water and thermometer are matter; their temperature is a property, not another substance.

preparation: Supply the ordinary material samples and original attributed fact cards above, plus blank has-mass/occupies-space/decision/reason fields. Given scientific facts can support this definition task; do not pretend classroom measurements occurred.

A safe trapped-air observation may illustrate occupied space. If a mass demonstration is used, an adult prepares an appropriate ball/balance with sufficient resolution and distinguishes the claim from a mouth-inflated-balloon comparison. No gas apparatus, force equation or independent weighing skill is required here.
learnerActions: Explain the two criteria in ordinary language, then apply both to the block, water and unseen air with reasons. Naming a state or saying particles alone is insufficient.
Classify the torch separately from its light, and the water separately from its temperature. Explain which is a material sample and why visibility or an illuminated region is not the criterion.

Change the context: move the same water to another-shaped container, or compare air trapped in a flexible bag with light passing through a window. State which material remains matter and whether the criterion depends on shape, being seen or being easily hefted.

Describe what evidence would help when a supplied case is genuinely insufficient; do not infer no mass merely because a classroom instrument cannot resolve a change. Retain the complete states task as a separate whole-claim check rather than score this portfolio as whole state/particle mastery.
successEvidence: Both criteria applied together to actual ordinary solid/liquid/gas examples, including unseen air.
Object/material distinguished from emitted light and a property with a source-supported explanation.
Reason persists across changed visibility/container/context rather than memorised labels.
nearMisses: Everything visible is matter but unseen air is nothing.
Only objects that keep shape are matter, or all things that move/affect something must be material.
The state-name or particle word is substituted for the two criteria.
An unresolvable balance difference is treated as proof of zero mass.
protocol.transfer: Original fictional claim: when clear air enters a bag and the torch illuminates it, neither is matter because neither is a solid object. Explain the different decisions for the actual air, bag and emitted light using the taught criteria and provided facts.

canonicalBoundary: Preserve every authored claim/guide and all existing intervals/standards. One source-specific component association is proposed; no new topic, dependency or age floor.
